subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices
title: Arjun's First Share: How the Stock Market Works
hook: When Arjun buys a tiny piece of a company, who sets the price? Let's follow the market.

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: His cousin, a stock broker in Mumbai

slides.title: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices
The Tea Company Needs Money
slides.storyContext: Arjun's favourite tea brand in Bangalore wants to expand. The owner splits the company into 1 million tiny pieces called 'shares' and sells them to raise ₹50 crore. Arjun buys 10 shares for ₹5,000. Now he owns a small piece of the company. Every day, buyers and sellers meet on the stock exchange to trade these shares. The price moves based on how many people want to buy vs. how many want to sell. Priya, his cousin, shows him the BSE platform.

slides.title: What is a Share (Equity)?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A share is a unit of ownership in a company. If a company has 1,00,000 shares and you own 100, you own 0.1% of the company.

points.label: Rights
points.text: Shareholders get voting rights (choose the board of directors) and a claim on profits (dividends), though not guaranteed.

points.label: Liquidity
points.text: Shares can be bought and sold on stock exchanges (BSE, NSE) during trading hours. You can convert shares to cash quickly.

slides.inSimpleWords: A share is a certificate of partial ownership. Buy shares, become part-owner; the company's profits are partly yours.

example.problem: Maruti Suzuki has 2 crore shares issued. Arjun buys 50 shares. What % of the company does he own?
example.solution: Arjun's ownership = 50 / (2 crore) = 50 / 2,00,00,000 = 0.000025% = 1 in 40 lakh shareholders.

slides.title: Supply & Demand Sets the Price

points.label: Price Discovery
points.text: On the stock exchange, buyers place 'bids' (offer price) and sellers place 'asks' (asking price). When bid matches ask, a trade happens at that price.

points.label: Demand ↑ = Price ↑
points.text: If 10,000 investors want to buy the tea stock but only 1,000 shares are for sale, the price rises. Scarcity increases value.

points.label: Supply ↑ = Price ↓
points.text: If a big shareholder dumps 50,000 shares on the market, prices often fall as supply floods demand.

slides.inSimpleWords: Price is decided by who wants to buy and who wants to sell. More buyers than sellers = higher price. More sellers than buyers = lower price.

example.problem: On Day 1, the tea stock opens at ₹100. By noon, 50,000 people want to buy but only 5,000 shares are on offer. By 2 PM it reaches ₹120. Why?
example.solution: Demand is 10x supply. Buyers are willing to pay higher prices to get shares. The price rises until enough buyers step back and enough sellers step forward to balance.

slides.title: The Stock Exchange: BSE & NSE

points.label: BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange)
points.text: India's oldest exchange (since 1875). Headquartered in Mumbai. Main index: Sensex (30 companies). Trading via licensed brokers.

points.label: NSE (National Stock Exchange)
points.text: Younger, electronic exchange (founded 1992). Main index: Nifty 50 (50 companies). More volumes, faster.

points.label: How It Works
points.text: You don't go to the exchange floor. You call a broker (online or human), place an order, and the broker matches you with a seller/buyer. The exchange records and settles the trade (T+1: trade day + 1, shares land in your account next day).

slides.inSimpleWords: BSE and NSE are electronic marketplaces. You use a broker to buy or sell. They find the other party, execute the trade, and settle it the next day.

slides.title: Types of Orders & Strategies

points.label: Market Order
points.text: Buy/sell immediately at whatever the current price is. Fast, but you don't control the exact price.

points.label: Limit Order
points.text: Set a price cap: 'Sell at ₹120 or higher, not lower.' It waits until that price is available or the order expires.

points.label: Stop-Loss Order
points.text: Protect yourself: 'If the price drops to ₹90, auto-sell.' Prevents big losses if the stock crashes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different order types give you different levels of control. Market order is fast. Limit order is precise. Stop-loss protects you from big drops.

example.problem: Arjun buys 100 shares at ₹100 = ₹10,000. He sets a stop-loss at ₹90. If the stock crashes to ₹85, what happens?
example.solution: The broker auto-sells the 100 shares at ₹90 (or the next best price), locking in a ₹10 loss per share = ₹1,000 total loss. Without the stop-loss, he might have lost ₹1,500 or more.

slides.title: Bid-Ask Spread & Brokers

points.label: Bid-Ask Spread
points.text: At any moment, the highest bid (buy price) might be ₹100 and the lowest ask (sell price) ₹100.50. That ₹0.50 gap is the spread — profit for market makers.

points.label: Broker Commission
points.text: Your broker takes a small fee (e.g. 0.1% of trade value) for matching you with the other party. ₹10,000 trade = ₹10 commission.

points.label: Impact on Returns
points.text: A ₹10,000 investment at 0.2% fees costs ₹20 immediately. High-frequency traders can't profit from 0.1% moves; long-term investors ignore the spread.

slides.inSimpleWords: Brokers and market makers take a tiny cut. The bid-ask spread is usually small for popular shares (liquid) and bigger for unpopular ones (illiquid).

slides.title: Worked Problem: Arjun's First Trade
slides.storyContext: Arjun sees the tea company's Q1 results are strong. He decides to buy 100 shares. Priya walks him through the entire trade.

points.label: Step 1: Research
points.text: Current price ₹100. Market cap ₹1,000 crore. P/E ratio 15. Priya says: 'Fair value is ₹100–110. Good time to buy.'

points.label: Step 2: Place Order
points.text: Arjun places a limit order: 'Buy 100 shares at max ₹102.' Within 2 minutes, 100 shares at ₹101 are matched. Cost = ₹10,100.

points.label: Step 3: Brokerage & Settlement
points.text: Broker charges ₹20 (0.2% of ₹10,100). Arjun pays ₹10,120 total. Next day (T+1), 100 shares appear in his demat account.

points.label: Step 4: Ownership
points.text: Arjun now holds a certificate: 'You own 100 units of Tea Co. Ltd.' He can vote in AGM, receive dividends, or sell anytime the market is open.

slides.inSimpleWords: Buying shares is like buying a fractional ownership certificate. Research the price, place an order, pay the broker fee, and own it next day.

slides.title: Challenge: Price Movements During Market Hours
slides.storyContext: It's 9:15 AM on a Monday. The tea stock opens at ₹100. By 10:30 AM, Arjun sees it's ₹105. He wonders: Should he still buy? His friend says the price might drop again by 3:30 PM.

points.label: The Scenario
points.text: Morning: stock at ₹105 (up 5%). Afternoon: slips to ₹102. End of day (3:30 PM): settles at ₹104. Q: What caused the intraday swings, and when is the 'best' time to buy?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Intraday price swings depend on news, sentiment, and volume. Morning surge might be profit-taking by overnight traders.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: No one can predict the best second to buy. But for long-term investors, the entry price within a 5% range doesn't matter much over 5 years.

example.problem: Arjun commits ₹10,000 to the tea stock. If he buys at ₹100 (100 shares) or ₹105 (95 shares), which is better if the stock reaches ₹200 in 5 years?
example.solution: At ₹100: 100 shares × ₹200 = ₹20,000 profit = 100% return. At ₹105: 95 shares × ₹200 = ₹19,000 profit = 90% return. Entry price matters for final returns, but both are good. Timing the exact low is impossible; dollar-cost averaging (buying in tranches) is smarter.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Ownership & Shares
points.text: A share = fractional ownership. Buy shares on BSE/NSE via a broker.

points.label: Price Discovery
points.text: Price = where supply meets demand. More buyers (or fewer sellers) = higher price.

points.label: The Mechanism
points.text: Brokers match buyers & sellers. T+1 settlement. Bid-ask spread & fees apply.

points.label: Order Types
points.text: Market order (fast), Limit order (precise), Stop-loss (protection).

points.label: Long-term Investing
points.text: Exact entry price matters less than 5-year hold. Diversify, don't time the market.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stock market is a place where fractional ownership of companies changes hands based on supply and demand. Understand the mechanism, use a broker, set stop-losses, and invest for the long term.

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices
title: Priya's Market Report: Reading Stock Prices & Indices
hook: The Sensex falls 200 points—what does it mean and who should care? Priya teaches Arjun to read the market.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Growing investor learning to read market data

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Stock broker and mentor from BSE Mumbai

characters.name: Mr. Desai
characters.role: Retired fund manager who explains indices

slides.title: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices
The Morning Market Report
slides.storyContext: Arjun opens the Economic Times on his phone. He reads: 'Sensex tumbles 200 points on profit-taking; Nifty holds 24,000 level.' He has no idea what it means. He calls Priya, who's at BSE watching the live tickers. She says, 'Sensex and Nifty are like the 'pulse' of the market. They tell you if India Inc. is healthy or anxious. Let me break it down for you step by step.'

slides.title: Stock Price vs. Market Capitalization

points.label: Stock Price (₹)
points.text: The price per share. A company might trade at ₹50/share or ₹2,000/share. The absolute price is not a measure of 'bigness.'

points.label: Market Cap = Price × Shares Outstanding
points.text: A better measure of company size. If TCS trades at ₹3,500 and has 350 crore shares, Market Cap = ₹12.25 lakh crore. Reliance at ₹2,500 with 180 crore shares = ₹4.5 lakh crore. TCS is bigger.

points.label: Why This Matters
points.text: You can't compare 'Is ₹50/share cheap vs. ₹2,000/share expensive?' without knowing the share count. Market cap is apples-to-apples.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock price alone is misleading. Market cap (price × total shares) tells you how big the company really is. A ₹50 stock with 1 billion shares is bigger than a ₹5,000 stock with 50 million shares.

example.problem: Stock A: ₹100/share, 10 crore shares. Stock B: ₹500/share, 1 crore shares. Which company is bigger?
example.solution: Stock A: Market Cap = ₹100 × 10 crore = ₹1,000 crore. Stock B: Market Cap = ₹500 × 1 crore = ₹500 crore. Stock A's company is 2x bigger, even though its per-share price is 1/5th.

slides.title: What is a Stock Index?

points.label: Definition
points.text: An index is a weighted basket of leading company stocks. Think of it as the 'representative sample' of the whole market. If the index is up, the market is generally up.

points.label: Purpose
points.text: Indices measure market health at a glance. You don't need to track all 5,000 listed companies; track the index instead.

points.label: Weighting
points.text: Indices are usually weighted by market cap. Bigger companies (higher market cap) have more influence on the index movement. TCS (₹12 lakh crore) moves Sensex more than a ₹1,000 crore micro-cap.

slides.inSimpleWords: An index is like the 'health report' of the stock market. It's a basket of top companies weighted by size. When Sensex goes up, it means the big companies are doing well.

slides.title: Sensex: The 30-Company Pulse (BSE)

points.label: 30 Largest Companies
points.text: Sensex = Bombay Stock Exchange Sensitive Index. It includes India's 30 largest companies (TCS, Reliance, HDFC Bank, Infosys, ITC, ICICI Bank, Bajaj, etc.).

points.label: Market-Cap Weighted
points.text: TCS (₹12+ lakh crore) has ~10% weight in Sensex. A ₹1,000 crore company has <0.1% weight. If TCS stock rises 5%, Sensex rises ~0.5%.

points.label: Historical Baseline
points.text: Jan 1, 1979 baseline = 100 points. Today, Sensex is 80,000+ points. It's gone up 800x in 45 years. A proxy for India's economic growth.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sensex = the top 30 Indian companies. If Sensex is up, India's best companies are making profits. If down, there's concern in the market.

example.problem: Sensex is 80,000 today. It was 70,000 a year ago. What's the annual return?
example.solution: Return = (80,000 - 70,000) / 70,000 = 10,000 / 70,000 = 14.3% annual appreciation (before dividends). This is the 'market return' for 2024.

slides.title: Nifty 50: The NSE's 50-Stock Index

points.label: NSE's Answer to Sensex
points.text: Nifty 50 = 50 largest companies on National Stock Exchange (NSE). Launched 1996. Includes Sensex stocks + 20 others (Bajaj Finance, Wipro, Maruti, NTPC, etc.).

points.label: Slightly Broader
points.text: 50 stocks vs. Sensex's 30 gives a wider view. But correlation is very high (~0.99). If Sensex up 2%, Nifty is usually up ~2%.

points.label: Mutual Fund Benchmark
points.text: Nifty 50 is the standard benchmark. 'Our fund returned 18% vs. Nifty's 16%' means it beat the market. If it returned 14% vs. Nifty 16%, it underperformed.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nifty 50 = top 50 Indian companies. Similar to Sensex but slightly broader. Most mutual funds measure themselves against Nifty.

slides.title: Reading the Daily Market Report

points.label: Sensex 80,000, up 200 points (+0.25%)
points.text: The 30-stock index closed at 80,000. It gained 200 points from yesterday's close. That's a 0.25% daily move (200/80,000). Normal volatility.

points.label: Volume: 500 million shares traded
points.text: Total shares traded across all 30 stocks = 500 million. High volume = high interest, more conviction in the move. Low volume = uncertain, could reverse.

points.label: Advance/Decline Ratio: 18 up, 12 down
points.text: Of the 30 stocks, 18 ended in green (profit), 12 in red (loss). Ratio 60:40 (up:down). A healthy day. If it's 29:1, that's 'euphoria.' If 1:29, that's a 'crash.'

points.label: Sector Performance
points.text: IT stocks +2%, Finance +1%, Pharma -0.5%. You can see which part of the economy is favored today.

slides.inSimpleWords: A market report tells you the index level, the points gained/lost, the volume (intensity), and the advance-decline ratio (how many stocks went up vs. down). All tell you the 'mood' of the market.

slides.title: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio & Valuation

points.label: P/E Ratio = Stock Price / Earnings Per Share (EPS)
points.text: TCS stock ₹3,500. Annual EPS ₹200. P/E = 3,500 / 200 = 17.5. Means: You're paying ₹17.50 for every ₹1 of annual earnings.

points.label: Market P/E vs. Stock P/E
points.text: Sensex's average P/E is ~20. If a stock's P/E is 15, it's undervalued (cheap). If 30, it's expensive (investors expect high future growth).

points.label: Interpretation
points.text: High P/E (>25) = expensive but high growth expected. Low P/E (<15) = cheap but may have risks or low growth. Average P/E (15–25) = fairly priced.

slides.inSimpleWords: P/E ratio shows how many rupees you pay per rupee of company earnings. Lower P/E = cheaper (potentially undervalued). Higher P/E = expensive (growth expected).

example.problem: Stock X: ₹1,000 price, ₹50 EPS. Stock Y: ₹2,000 price, ₹100 EPS. Which is cheaper?
example.solution: Stock X P/E = 1,000/50 = 20. Stock Y P/E = 2,000/100 = 20. Both have the same valuation! Per-share price alone is misleading.

slides.title: Reading a Stock Quote: Detailed Breakdown
slides.storyContext: Arjun looks at TCS's live quote on his broker's app. Priya walks him through every number.

points.label: Current Price: ₹3,680
points.text: The last traded price. Real-time, updated every second during market hours (9:15 AM–3:30 PM, Monday–Friday).

points.label: 52-Week High: ₹4,100 | 52-Week Low: ₹2,800
points.text: TCS's highest and lowest price in the past 52 weeks. Currently trading near the high, suggesting optimism.

points.label: Market Cap: ₹12.85 lakh crore
points.text: The company's total value. TCS is India's largest IT company by market cap.

points.label: P/E Ratio: 18 | Industry Average: 22
points.text: TCS is cheaper than average IT stock. Might be undervalued or facing near-term headwinds.

points.label: Dividend Yield: 1.2%
points.text: TCS pays ₹44/share annual dividend. ₹44 / ₹3,680 = 1.2%. Plus capital appreciation, this is total return.

points.label: Volume (10M shares traded today)
points.text: High volume = liquid, easy to buy/sell. Low volume = illiquid, wider bid-ask spread, risk of slippage.

slides.inSimpleWords: A stock quote shows price, valuation, dividends, and trading activity. High 52-week high = stock doing well. Low P/E relative to peers = potentially undervalued. High volume = easy to exit.

slides.title: Challenge: Comparing Two Stocks
slides.storyContext: Arjun wants to invest ₹50,000 in either Bank A or Bank B. He pulls up their quotes. Bank A: ₹500/share, Market Cap ₹5 lakh crore, P/E 12. Bank B: ₹2,000/share, Market Cap ₹8 lakh crore, P/E 18. He calls Mr. Desai for advice.

points.label: The Question
points.text: Based on price alone, Bank B (₹2,000) looks 'expensive' vs. Bank A (₹500). Is Bank B really expensive, or is it just higher-priced?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Don't compare per-share prices directly. Compare market caps and P/E ratios.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: A lower P/E means lower expectations for growth, or market is pessimistic. A higher P/E means growth is expected.

example.problem: Using the above data, which stock offers better value: Bank A (P/E 12) or Bank B (P/E 18)?
example.solution: Bank A has a lower P/E (12 vs. 18), so it's cheaper relative to earnings. You're paying ₹12 per ₹1 of earnings at Bank A vs. ₹18 at Bank B. Bank A looks undervalued unless Bank B is expected to grow faster. Check recent profit growth and guidance before deciding.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Market Cap, Not Price
points.text: Use market cap to compare company size, not per-share price.

points.label: Sensex & Nifty
points.text: Sensex (30 stocks, BSE) and Nifty (50 stocks, NSE) are benchmarks for market health. Both move together.

points.label: P/E Ratio
points.text: P/E = Price / Earnings. Low P/E = cheap (but risky). High P/E = expensive (but growth expected).

points.label: Daily Report
points.text: Read index points, volume, advance-decline, and sector moves. They tell the market's mood.

points.label: Stock Quote
points.text: Price, 52-week range, P/E, market cap, dividend yield, volume — all are clues to value and liquidity.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use market cap and P/E ratios to compare stocks fairly. Watch Sensex/Nifty for market trend. Read the daily report to understand which sectors are in favor. A lower P/E isn't always 'cheap'—it depends on growth prospects.

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money
title: Rohini's Safe Returns: Understanding Bonds & Fixed Income
hook: Instead of owning a company (equity), lend money to one and get guaranteed interest. Let's explore fixed income.

characters.name: Arjun
characters.role: Young investor learning balance between stocks and bonds

characters.name: Mrs. Sharma
characters.role: Retiree living on bond interest and FD income

slides.title: Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money
The Tea Company Needs a Loan
slides.storyContext: The tea company wants to build a new factory. Instead of selling more shares, the manager decides to borrow ₹100 crore from investors by issuing bonds. Rohini, a school principal near Pune, buys ₹5 lakh worth of these bonds. The company promises to pay her 7% interest annually for 10 years, then return the ₹5 lakh at the end. Unlike stocks (where she becomes part-owner), bonds are a loan. She gets fixed, predictable interest every year regardless of company profits. Mrs. Sharma, her retired neighbour, does the same. They both sleep soundly knowing ₹35,000 is coming their way next month, like clockwork.

slides.title: What is a Bond?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A bond is a loan. A company (or government) borrows money from you and promises to pay interest (coupon) periodically and return the principal at maturity.

points.label: Coupon (Interest)
points.text: Fixed interest rate, e.g. 7% per annum. A ₹1 lakh bond at 7% pays ₹7,000/year, either in one lump sum or in tranches (e.g. ₹3,500 twice yearly).

points.label: Maturity (Tenure)
points.text: Time period, e.g. 5 years, 10 years, 20 years. At maturity, the company returns your principal. No early exit without selling in the secondary market.

points.label: Equity vs. Bond
points.text: Equity = ownership, risky, variable returns, high upside. Bond = lending, safer, fixed returns, lower upside. A balanced portfolio has both.

slides.inSimpleWords: A bond is like lending money to a company. You get fixed interest (coupon) every year and get your money back after the agreed period (maturity). Less risky than stocks, but lower potential returns.

example.problem: Rohini buys a ₹5 lakh bond at 7% coupon, 10-year maturity. How much will she receive in total?
example.solution: Annual interest = ₹5 lakh × 7% = ₹35,000. Over 10 years = ₹35,000 × 10 = ₹3.5 lakh. Plus principal = ₹5 lakh + ₹3.5 lakh = ₹8.5 lakh total received. Net gain = ₹3.5 lakh (if she holds to maturity and there's no default).

slides.title: Bond Pricing & Yield

points.label: Par Value vs. Market Price
points.text: Par value = ₹1 lakh (face value). Market price = what you pay to buy it. If interest rates ↑, older bonds (with lower coupons) drop in price. If rates ↓, older bonds become attractive and rise.

points.label: Yield
points.text: Current Yield = Annual Coupon / Current Market Price. Example: ₹1 lakh bond at 7% coupon, now trading at ₹95,000. Yield = ₹7,000 / ₹95,000 = 7.37%. If interest rates were 8%, the bond trades at a discount.

points.label: Inverse Relationship
points.text: Bond Price ↑ when interest rates ↓ (bond becomes valuable). Bond Price ↓ when interest rates ↑ (new bonds offer more coupon, old ones worth less). This is critical for bond trading and duration risk.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bond prices move inversely with interest rates. When rates fall, bond prices rise (old bonds with fixed coupon become more valuable). When rates rise, bond prices fall (new bonds offer better returns).

example.problem: A 10-year bond has ₹1 lakh par, 6% coupon. Central bank raises rates to 8%. Why does the bond's market price fall?
example.solution: New bonds now offer 8% coupon. The old 6% bond is less attractive. To make it competitive, its price must fall so the yield equals 8%. If new price = ₹75,000, yield = ₹6,000 / ₹75,000 = 8%. That's now equivalent.

slides.title: Types of Bonds in India

points.label: Government Securities (G-Sec)
points.text: Issued by the Indian government. Backed by sovereign credit (lowest risk). 10-year G-Sec yields 6–7%. E.g. US Treasury, Indian Treasury bills (Tbills). PSU Bonds: Issued by public sector units (NTPC, Power Finance Corp). Yield 7–8%, slightly higher risk than G-Sec.

points.label: Corporate Bonds
points.text: Issued by private companies (TCS, Reliance, Infosys). Yield 8–10%, more risk. Credit rating matters: AAA (safest) to D (default imminent). Lower-rated bonds offer higher coupon to compensate for risk.

points.label: Savings Schemes (RBI-backed)
points.text: NSC (National Savings Certificate): 8% interest, 5-year lock-in, tax benefits. Senior Citizen Savings Scheme: 8.2% for ages 60+. PPF (Public Provident Fund): 7.1%, 15-year tenure, tax-free. Sukanya Samriddhi: 8.2% for girl child, 21-year tenure.

slides.inSimpleWords: Government bonds = safest, lowest yield (~6%). Corporate bonds = higher yield (~8–10%) but more risky. Choose based on your risk appetite and timeline.

slides.title: Fixed Deposits (FDs): The Bank's Bond

points.label: What is an FD?
points.text: You deposit a lump sum with a bank for a fixed period (3 months to 10 years). The bank guarantees a fixed interest rate and returns your principal + interest at maturity.

points.label: Interest Rates (as of 2024)
points.text: Banks offer 6–7.5% on 1-year FDs. Senior citizens get +0.5% (e.g. 7.5% → 8%). Rates vary by bank and tenure. SBI might offer 6.5%, ICICI 7%, a private bank 7.5%.

points.label: Liquidity
points.text: Money is locked. Early withdrawal = penalty (lose interest, pay fee). Cannot be traded like bonds. But very safe (DICGC insures up to ₹5 lakh per account per bank).

points.label: Tax
points.text: Interest is taxable as income. A ₹1 lakh FD at 7% yields ₹7,000 interest. If your tax rate is 30%, after-tax return = ₹7,000 × 70% = ₹4,900 (4.9% after-tax yield).

slides.inSimpleWords: FD = locked savings with guaranteed interest. Safe, insured by the bank, but not tradeable and early exit attracts a penalty. Interest is taxable.

example.problem: Mrs. Sharma deposits ₹10 lakh in a 5-year FD at 7% (compounded annually). How much will she receive at maturity?
example.solution: Using compound interest: A = P(1 + r/100)^n = 10,00,000 × (1.07)^5 = 10,00,000 × 1.4026 = ₹14,02,552. Interest earned = ₹4,02,552. More than simple interest (which would be ₹3.5 lakh).

slides.title: Bonds vs. FDs vs. Stocks

points.label: Bond
points.text: Tradeable (can sell mid-term in secondary market). Interest rate fixed, but price fluctuates with rate changes. Yield varies by credit rating. Maturity can be 5–30 years. Can earn capital gains if rates fall and you sell.

points.label: FD
points.text: Not tradeable (locked). Interest rate fixed, principal stable. Insured up to ₹5 lakh. Early exit = penalty. Tenure 3 months–10 years. No capital gains; interest is only return.

points.label: Stock (Equity)
points.text: Highly tradeable, very liquid. No fixed interest (but dividends sometimes). Price very volatile, can swing 20%+ in a week. Long-term returns ~12–15% but with high volatility. Can make capital gains or losses.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock = own a piece, high risk, high reward. Bond = lend and collect interest, tradeable, medium risk. FD = lend to bank, locked, safe, lowest reward.

slides.title: Duration & Interest Rate Risk

points.label: Duration
points.text: Measure of how sensitive a bond's price is to interest rate changes. A 10-year bond has higher duration than a 2-year bond. When rates ↑, long-duration bonds fall sharply in price.

points.label: Interest Rate Risk
points.text: If you buy a 10-year bond at 6% and rates rise to 8%, your bond's value drops (because new bonds offer 8%). You're 'underwater.' If you hold to maturity, you get full principal back; but if you need to sell early, you lose money.

points.label: Ladder Strategy
points.text: Spread purchases across different maturities: buy 1-year, 3-year, 5-year, 10-year bonds. As short-term bonds mature, reinvest at new (possibly higher) rates. Avoids lock-in at low rates.

slides.inSimpleWords: Longer bonds have more interest rate risk. When rates rise, long-term bond prices fall sharply. To reduce risk, buy bonds with different maturities (ladder).

example.problem: Rohini buys a 5-year bond at ₹1 lakh, 6% coupon. After 2 years, rates rise to 8%. She needs to sell. What happens?
example.solution: Bond has 3 years left. Its 6% coupon is now unattractive vs. new 8% bonds. Price drops to ~₹95,000 so yield ≈ 8%. She realizes a ₹5,000 loss if she sells. But if she holds 3 more years, she gets full ₹1 lakh principal back.

slides.title: Worked Problem: Rohini's Portfolio Balancing
slides.storyContext: Rohini has ₹30 lakh to invest. She's 45 years old, working for 20 more years. She asks Mrs. Sharma and Arjun how to split it.

points.label: Arjun's Suggestion (Young & Aggressive)
points.text: 60% stocks, 40% bonds. Rationale: 20-year horizon allows riding volatility. Stocks historically deliver 12%+ CAGR. Bonds provide stability. Annual rebalance.

points.label: Mrs. Sharma's Suggestion (Retired & Conservative)
points.text: 80% bonds/FDs, 20% stocks. At 70+, needs steady income. Can't afford to lose capital. Lives on interest. FDs + G-Secs provide ₹2+ lakh annual income (7% on ₹30 lakh).

points.label: Rohini's Decision (Balanced)
points.text: 50% stocks (₹15 lakh): TCS, Infosys, HDFC Bank for growth. 40% bonds (₹12 lakh): Mix of G-Sec (6%), corporate bonds (8%), PSU bonds (7.5%). 10% FD (₹3 lakh): Emergency buffer, liquid.

points.label: Expected Returns
points.text: Stocks: 15 lakh × 12% = ₹1.8 lakh. Bonds: 12 lakh × 7.5% = ₹0.9 lakh. FD: 3 lakh × 6.5% = ₹1.95 lakh (after compounding). Annual portfolio return ~₹4.65 lakh (weighted ~10.5% CAGR).

slides.inSimpleWords: Diversification across stocks, bonds, and FDs balances risk and return. Young investors can afford more stocks; older investors prefer bonds. Adjust based on age and goals.

slides.title: Challenge: Credit Rating & Default Risk
slides.storyContext: Arjun compares two corporate bonds: Bond A (TCS, rated AAA) at 7% yield; Bond B (a smaller IT company, rated BBB) at 10% yield. He asks, 'Why should I accept 7% from TCS when I can get 10% from the smaller company?'

points.label: The Dilemma
points.text: Higher yield = higher risk. Bond B's 10% looks attractive, but what if the company defaults and Arjun loses principal?

points.label: Hint 1
points.text: Credit rating reflects default probability. AAA = <0.01% default risk. BBB = ~0.5% default risk. The yield compensates for that risk.

points.label: Hint 2
points.text: In a recession, BBB companies struggle first. AAA companies weather it. During COVID, many small-cap bonds defaulted; blue-chip bonds held.

example.problem: Bond A (AAA, TCS): ₹1 lakh, 7% yield, 0.1% default probability. Bond B (BBB, small IT): ₹1 lakh, 10% yield, 1% default probability. Expected return?
example.solution: Bond A: (1 lakh × 1.07) × 99.9% + (0 × 0.1%) = ₹1.07 lakh (99.9% chance). Expected = ₹1.0693 lakh. Bond B: (1 lakh × 1.10) × 99% + (0 × 1%) = ₹1.089 lakh (99% chance). Expected = ₹1.0791 lakh. Difference: ₹1 lakh. Risk-reward is roughly similar, but Bond B has a tail risk (1% chance of ₹1 lakh loss). Choose based on risk tolerance.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.label: Bonds: Lending to Companies
points.text: You lend, they pay interest (coupon) and return principal at maturity. Fixed, predictable income.

points.label: Bond Pricing
points.text: Bond price ↑ when rates ↓, and vice versa. Long-term bonds have more price risk (duration).

points.label: Types: G-Sec, Corporate, Bonds, PSU, FDs, Savings Schemes
points.text: G-Secs safest (~6% yield). Corporate bonds higher-yielding (~8–10%) but with default risk. FDs are bank loans, locked but insured.

points.label: FD Specifics
points.text: Safe, insured up to ₹5 lakh, illiquid, no trading. Interest is taxable. Best for emergency funds and retirees.

points.label: Diversification
points.text: Mix stocks, bonds, FDs based on age & goals. Young = more stocks. Older = more bonds/FDs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fixed income (bonds, FDs) offers steady returns with lower risk than stocks. Use them for stability and retirement planning. Credit rating matters—higher-rated bonds are safer but lower-yielding. Diversify across all three asset classes for balanced growth.
